doc_name: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes (Buenos Aires)
text: The National Museum of Fine Arts (Spanish: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes) is an Argentine art museum located in Buenos Aires, in the Recoleta section. It opened on 25 December 1895 in a building on Florida Street, which is now home to the Galerías Pacífico shopping mall. Eduardo Schiaffino, an Argentine painter and art critic, was its first director. In 1909, the museum moved to a building in Plaza San Martín, originally constructed in Paris as the Argentine Pavilion for the 1889 Paris exhibition, which was later dismantled and relocated to Buenos Aires. The museum participated in the International Centenary Exhibition in Buenos Aires in 1910. After the pavilion was demolished in 1932 as part of Plaza San Martín's remodeling, the museum relocated to its current site in 1943, a building initially built in 1870 as a drainage pumping station and adapted for its use by architect Alejandro Bustillo. During the 1955–64 period under director Jorge Romero Brest, the museum underwent physical and collection modernization. A temporary exhibits pavilion opened in 1961, and the museum acquired a significant amount of modern art through collaboration with the Torcuato di Tella Institute and other sources; a contemporary Argentine art pavilion opened in 1980. This 1,536 square metres (16,533 sq ft) hall is the largest of 34 currently in use, with the museum’s total exhibit space amounting to 4,610 square metres (49,622 sq ft). Its permanent collection includes 688 major works and over 12,000 sketches, fragments, potteries, and other minor works. The institution also maintains a specialized library with 150,000 volumes and a public auditorium. The museum commissioned architect Mario Roberto Álvarez to design a branch in Neuquén, inaugurated in 2004, which features four exhibit halls totaling 2,500 square metres (26,910 sq ft), a permanent collection of 215 works, temporary exhibits, and a public auditorium. The ground floor contains 24 exhibit halls with a fine international collection of paintings from the Middle Ages to the 20th century, along with the museum’s art history library. The first floor has eight exhibit halls showcasing works by prominent 20th-century Argentine painters, including Antonio Berni, Ernesto de la Cárcova, Benito Quinquela Martín, Eduardo Sívori, Sarah Grilo, Alfredo Guttero, Raquel Forner, Xul Solar, Marcelo Pombo, and Lino Enea Spilimbergo. The second floor, with two halls completed in 1984, features a photography exhibition, two sculpture terraces, and houses most of the institution’s administrative and technical departments.
